Soleiman Faqiri, une mort qui ne s’expli: Soleiman Faqiri, a death that can’t be explained
Soleiman était détenu depuis 11 jours po: Soleiman had been held for 11 days for reasons his family still doesn’t understand.
« Toutes les familles canadiennes compte: “Every Canadian family has a Soleiman among them,” says Yusuf Faqiri, pointing out that many people in this country live with mental health problems like his late brother. He hopes, however, that they won’t be incarcerated. “It forced me to act,” he says. He became an activist after Soleiman’s death five years ago. “People with mental illness shouldn’t be in prison; they should be in hospital. Soleiman didn’t need to be in prison.
Cette tragédie aurait pu être évitée à 1: This tragedy was 100 per cent preventable,” Yusuf believes. Soleiman Faqiri died in 2016 at the hands of correctional staff at the Central East Correctional Centre (CECC) in Lindsay, Ontario. He was 30. Passing through his former province, Yusuf tells us the story of Soli, as his family calls him, so that it won’t happen again. “Tomorrow, someone’s remains will be handed over to their family. That’s why we have to tell how a 30-year-old man with his whole life ahead of him, a brother, a son, a brilliant mind, was murdered, beaten to death.”
Soleiman était détenu depuis 11 jours po: Soleiman had been held for 11 days for reasons his family doesn’t understand. No charges had been laid against him. Behind bars, he was waiting to be transferred to a psychiatric facility, a transfer that had been granted three days earlier. On December 15, 2016, correctional officers entered his cell. Soleiman would not come out alive. In a report released last August, Dr. Michael Pollanen, Ontario’s chief forensic pathologist, determined that Mr. Faqiri succumbed to his injuries after being held face down and beaten by correctional officers.
« Il avait 50 bleus sur le corps, ses ja: “He had 50 bruises on his body, his legs and hands were shackled, he was pepper-sprayed twice,” Yusuf lists. Two investigations have already been carried out, with no charges laid. The coroner’s office had previously concluded that the cause of Soleiman Faqiri’s death was “undetermined.” Following the revelations in this new report, a third investigation, led by the Ontario Provincial Police, is under way. “It was the guards who took his life, not schizophrenia,” says Yusuf Faqiri. For the victim’s brother, it has been a constant battle since his brother Soli was arrested. “I also made myself a promise that I would not let my brother’s murder be the last word in his story. That he was more than that, that he was more than his illness. That he was more than his tragic end,” Yusuf confides.

Yusuf est l’aîné de sa famille, qui comp: Yusuf is the eldest of five siblings. Soleiman is the second-youngest brother, two years younger than Yusuf. “We always had that rivalry between brothers,” Yusuf says, growing animated. He describes his brother as a brilliant man who, unlike him, excelled at school. Soleiman was captain of the football team and also played rugby in high school.
« Ce sont les choses dont j’aime me souv: “Those are the things I like to remember,” Yusuf says of his brother. “But it wasn’t just his talents. He was a very kind man.”
Il raconte comment, lorsque sa mère est: He recounts how, when their mother fell ill after their little brother was born, Soleiman, himself still a child, changed diapers and prepared bottles of formula.
Plus tard, le jeune homme a appris à sa: Later, the young man taught his mother to read, and Yusuf to pray. One of Yusuf’s earliest memories dates back to his early childhood, when he and his family were fleeing the civil war in Afghanistan. Throughout the journey, during which the family had to hide, Yusuf held the hand of his little brother Soli. The Faqiris sought refuge in Canada, and Soleiman and Yusuf grew up in Ontario, in the Durham region.
Yusuf et Soleiman Faqiri, en Ontario. Ph: Yusuf and Soleiman Faqiri, in Ontario. Photo: Courtesy of Yusuf Faqiri
En 2005, à l’âge de 19 ans, Soleiman reç: In 2005, at the age of 19, Soleiman was diagnosed with schizophrenia. Despite the stigma, his family did not let it break them. “My mother gathered the family and said, ‘You are going to accept my son as he is,’” Yusuf recalls. “She placed Soleiman’s personality within his story, before the mental illness. She didn’t want his illness to define him.” It was this attitude, combined with family support, that allowed the young man to thrive over the next 11 years. “It wasn’t perfect, there were challenges,” adds Yusuf, his voice choked with emotion. “What kept him alive for 11 years [after being diagnosed] was my mother.”
« Il était un membre indispensable de la: “He was an indispensable member of the family. We became better people because of him,” he says of the man he describes as complex, a son, a brother, a wonderful human being. “And that’s what I want the world to remember.” Time passes, and the wound is still as raw for the Faqiris. “I’m not used to my brother being gone, I have to accept it. I’m not going to let the police or the justice system have the last word, we will have the last word,” says Yusuf. A few weeks after Soleiman’s death, his brother asked a friend to help him create a Facebook page, which they named <l1>Justice for Soli</l1>. Since then, the <l2>organization</l2> he created has travelled across the country to give talks and has given more than a hundred interviews to Canadian media.
« Le mouvement est devenu beaucoup plus: “The movement has become much bigger than we could have expected. But that was not our intention,” explains the founder. For him, it’s about something more than Soleiman’s death. “His case has become a catalyst for instituting change for individuals with mental illness in the prison and police systems,” he says. For Yusuf, who is in contact with families and loved ones of victims, it is a systemic problem across the province and the country. “Unfortunately, prisons have become the new hospitals,” he says, pointing to the lack of resources and support for citizens. “It seems that the lives of people with mental health disorders are worth nothing.”
Soleiman Faqiri se trouvait chez sa sœur: Soleiman Faqiri was at his sister’s home in Ajax when he was arrested. He was alone in the residence. The family still doesn’t know why he was arrested or why he was placed in detention. “We don’t know who called the police,” says his brother. During the 11 days Soleiman was held, the family was never able to see him, despite four visits. “I went there to tell the staff about his mental health condition,” Yusuf says. Three days before Soleiman’s death, a judge ordered that he be transferred to a psychiatric facility to be assessed and treated. Yusuf, who testified at the hearing, saw Soleiman on a screen, as he attended by videoconference. It would be the last time. Two hours after the testimony, the transfer request was made.
« Nous étions donc tous d’accord pour di: “So we all agreed that my brother shouldn’t be incarcerated, that he needed care,” says Yusuf. If Soleiman then had to wait in detention, it was because there was no bed available. He died three days later. Throughout his detention, the Faqiri family had to scramble to get information. “That’s how a lot of people end up dying. The system makes no effort to give information to the family. It’s a system that is closed in on itself and lacks transparency,” he says of the lack of communication. The only time the authorities reached out to the Faqiri family was when Soleiman died. “Two police officers came and said that Soli was dead after guards had entered his cell,” Yusuf remembers.

Les autres cas de personnes souffrant de: Yusuf knows by heart the other cases of people with mental health conditions who have died in custody in recent years. Last December, the case of Tamara Lucier, 31, reopened many wounds. The young woman died while in custody at the South West Detention Centre in Windsor, Ontario, in circumstances that recall Soleiman’s story.
Au moment de sa mort, elle attendait d’ê: At the time of her death, she was waiting to be treated in a psychiatric facility. No charges had been laid against her. Yusuf Faqiri also cites Jordan Sheard, Cleve “Cas” Geddes, Ashley Smith, Edward Snowshoe, Moses Beaver and Justin St. Amour, who died in custody and were living with mental health conditions. He adds the names of Nicholas Gibbs, Regis Korchinski-Paquet, Andrew Loku and Abdurahman Hassan, people struggling with mental health issues who died during interventions by law enforcement. And the list keeps growing.
« Il y a une intersection entre la malad: “There is an intersection between mental illness and corrections, but also between policing and mental illness, and it proves fatal,” says Yusuf. “The people in power at every level of government need to realize that this is a crisis, and that to resolve this crisis, systemic change is needed.”
Se fondant sur ses recherches, il estime: Based on his research, he estimates that more than 100 people with mental health problems have died in federal and provincial prisons. There are no official figures on this – a trend that can be observed at other levels of the correctional system. When asked about it, Correctional Service Canada (CSC) told us it has no data on the number of deaths of inmates with mental health problems. A <l1>report</l1> on violence in Ontario’s correctional institutions, released in 2018, states that there “[...] is clearly a need to improve the practices of the Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services (MCSCS) when it comes to data collection and information sharing.”
Un <l1>rapport</l1> paru en 2021 et inti: A 2021 <l1>report</l1> titled “<l2>Do Independent External Decision Makers Ensure that ‘An Inmate’s Confinement in a Structured Intervention Unit Is to End as Soon as Possible’?</l2>” written by criminologist Anthony N. Doob, examines how CSC’s structured intervention units (SIUs), which were meant to replace solitary confinement, operate. Soleiman Faqiri, like Tamara Lucier and Ashley Smith, was in isolation at the time of his death.
« Il semble que la santé mentale d’un in: “It appears that an individual’s mental health – or the mental health indicator used by CSC – does not play an important role in determining whether an SIU is an appropriate place for an individual to stay,” the report reads. Christi Thompson is an investigative reporter for <l1>The Marshall Project</l1>, a news outlet that covers the American criminal justice system. “It’s a major problem in the United States, people with severe mental illness who clearly need psychiatric hospitalization and care and who end up in prison.”
La journaliste estime que les institutio: The journalist believes that correctional institutions are not equipped to deal with people who have these health problems. “This kind of nightmare scenario where someone who should be in a hospital ends up in prison and dies is in some way the result of a larger problem, namely that people with serious mental illness are being incarcerated instead of treated,” she says. In the United States, a correctional officer’s mental health training depends on where they work, the journalist adds.
« Il devrait y avoir des psychiatres, de: “There should be psychiatrists, psychologists and nurses on staff. But how often these people are present in the facility and closely monitoring individuals varies a great deal,” Ms. Thompson observes, adding that the staff on site don’t have the resources a psychiatric facility would have to intervene, treat and keep the person safe. She also points to the lack of data on the prison system in the United States. “It’s very difficult to get a national count of how often these deaths [of people with mental health conditions] occur, in part because it can be very hard to get information about deaths in custody in general,” she explains. “That continues to be a major obstacle and challenge for journalists.”

« Combien de personnes vulnérables doive: “How many more vulnerable people have to die?” laments Yusuf Faqiri. “They need help, support, empathy, to be listened to, to be cared for. They must be looked after with honour and dignity, rather than being murdered, killed or put in cages.” He wants people with mental health conditions to be entrusted to professionals who have the right tools to care for them. “The situation is likely to happen again,” he says. “Soleiman’s case clearly shows the problem that mental illness and incarceration represent. That’s why I keep telling this story, to make sure another family doesn’t go through the same thing,” says Yusuf. While he still wants the correctional officers who beat Soleiman to death to be held criminally responsible for their actions, he has few illusions left about that.
Ces derniers continuent à travailler. «: They are still working. “I’ve lost faith in the justice system. But I haven’t lost faith in my fellow citizens,” says Yusuf, who sees this fight as a way of giving back to society, but also of honouring the memory of his brother and of the others who are gone.
Le jeune homme demande un mécanisme tran: He is calling for a transparent and accountable mechanism, and for people with mental health conditions to be valued for who they are, rather than being seen as victims. “The system is broken. It hands out coffins,” he lets fall, before adding that he wants to make it a political and electoral issue. “My brother deserved a better end, just like the other families. The system ripped away fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters who deserved to be respected and treated with dignity.
Ils ont perdu la vie parce que leur vie: They lost their lives because their lives were considered worthless, because they had mental health conditions. And we have to put an end to this disaster,” he urges.
Malgré tout, Yusuf a l’impression que, a: Despite everything, Yusuf feels that, over time, more attention is being paid to these tragedies. Is it a sign of greater openness to mental health issues? “I believe mental illness is not a question of region, culture, ethnicity or gender. It’s a problem that affects all of us. If there’s one thing I’ve noticed over the last five years, it’s that people want to understand, to learn and to help their fellow citizens.”
